drills.title: Days until the sale ends
drills.prompt: Arrange the lines into a program that counts the days from 16 Nov 2026 to the end of the Diwali sale on 25 Nov 2026. Two lines do not belong.
drills.explain: Imports come first and name the full path of each class: ChronoUnit lives in java.time.temporal, not directly in java.time. LocalDate has no public constructor, you get one from a factory method such as LocalDate.of(year, month, day). ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(a, b) counts the days from a to b.

drills.title: Parse, format, add a week
drills.prompt: Fill the blanks so the program turns the text into a date, prints it as 25 Dec 2026, then shows the date a week later and its weekday.
drills.explain: LocalDate.parse reads text in the form yyyy-MM-dd (LocalDate.of takes three numbers instead). In a pattern, capital M is the month and lowercase m is the minute: MMM gives the short name Dec, MM would give 12. plusDays(7) returns a new date, because java.time objects never change.

drills.title: Does plusDays change the date?
drills.prompt: Read the code and type exactly what it prints, one line per line of output.
drills.explain: java.time objects are immutable: plusDays builds a new date and leaves the old one alone. The call on line 5 creates 17 Nov and throws it away, so today is still 16 Nov. Only later, which stored the result of plusDays(30), holds 16 Dec.

drills.title: A date the parser cannot read
drills.prompt: The customer typed the date as 16/11/2026, and the program crashes when it runs. Click the faulty line, then choose the fix.
drills.explain: LocalDate.parse(text) without a formatter only understands yyyy-MM-dd, so the slashes make it throw DateTimeParseException at run time. Give it a formatter that describes your text: dd/MM/yyyy. Lowercase mm means minutes, and MM/dd would read 16 as the month. LocalDate.of takes numbers, not text.

drills.title: Review the AI's reminder helpers
drills.prompt: An AI assistant wrote these date helpers. They compile and run, but tick the real problems (there are three).
code: static long daysLeft(LocalDate from, LocalDate to) {

issues.text: The pattern uses YYYY for the year
issues.why: YYYY is the week-based year. Around New Year it prints the wrong year (29 Dec 2026 would show 2027). Use yyyy for the normal calendar year.

issues.text: ofPattern("dd MMM ...") is called without a Locale
issues.why: MMM prints a month name in the computer's language, so Nov can come out as nov. or Nov. on another machine. Pass Locale.ENGLISH as the second argument.

issues.text: dueDate ignores the result of plusDays and returns the original date
issues.why: Dates are immutable, so start.plusDays(30) builds a new date and drops it. The method returns start unchanged (the output says 0 days). Write return start.plusDays(30).

non_issues.text: daysLeft returns long, so it should return int
non_issues.why: ChronoUnit.between returns a long on purpose, because a span of days can be big. Narrowing it to int would be the questionable choice.

non_issues.text: main uses LocalDate.of(...) instead of LocalDate.now()
non_issues.why: A fixed date makes the demo repeat exactly. The helpers take the date as a parameter, which is what lets you test them with fixed dates.

non_issues.text: The three imports should be replaced by import java.time.*
non_issues.why: java.time.* does not include the sub-packages format and temporal, so those imports would still be needed. Naming each class is fine.

non_issues.text: The helpers should be instance methods
non_issues.why: They use only their parameters and keep no state, so static methods are the right choice.

drills.explain: With dates, check every pattern letter (yyyy, MM vs mm, MMM plus a Locale) and every call that returns a new object: if its result is not stored or returned, nothing happened.
